challenges.name: rate-limit-submissions-quiz
challenges.title: Who should a submission limit count?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the mock exam day: the gateway's 429 log for a university lab and one scripted learner, and a Redis token bucket whose key expires after 10 seconds.

questions.question:
Gateway rule for POST /submissions on the mock exam day:

limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=submit_ip:10m rate=10r/s;
limit_req zone=submit_ip burst=20 nodelay;

Access log, 10:00-10:10, grouped:

client_ip        user_id        requests  429s
203.0.113.40     (118 learners)    7,412  1,870   <- university lab behind one NAT address
198.51.100.23    learner-8812      2,960      0   <- a userscript that re-submits every 200 ms

The API knows the learner's id from the access token before it handles the request.

Statement: "Keying the submission limit on the signed-in learner's id (for example 5 tokens, refilling 1 every 5 s) would stop the 429s for the lab while still limiting learner-8812's script."
questions.explanation: True. The lab's 118 learners share one address, so a per-IP limit adds their traffic together: 7,412 requests in 10 minutes is about 12 per second for the whole room, but only about 0.1 per second per learner, far below 1 every 5 s. The script is a single learner sending about 5 per second (2,960 in 600 s) from its own address, which stays under the 10 r/s per IP and is why it never got a 429. A per-learner bucket of 5 tokens refilling 0.2 per second lets each lab learner submit freely and gives the script about 1 submission every 5 s after its first 5. The misconception is that an IP address identifies a user: NAT, campus and mobile networks put many people behind one address, and one person can use many. Keep a stricter per-IP limit only for anonymous traffic, where the IP is all you have.

questions.question:
A pull request moves the per-learner token bucket (capacity 5, refill 0.2 tokens per second) to Redis. To save memory it sets a TTL on every bucket key:

-- KEYS[1] = ratelimit:submit:user:<id>   (a hash: tokens, last_ms)
-- ... refill, take a token or reject ...
redis.call("HSET", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens, "last_ms", now_ms)
redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], 10000)   -- forget buckets idle for 10 s

A missing key is treated as a new, full bucket.

Statement: "The 10-second TTL only saves memory; it cannot change which requests get a 429."
questions.explanation: False. An empty bucket needs 5 / 0.2 = 25 seconds to refill completely, but its key disappears after 10 idle seconds and the next request finds a new, full bucket. A learner who spends 5 tokens, waits 10 seconds and repeats gets 5 submissions every 10 s (0.5 per second) instead of 5 + 10 x 0.2 = 7 in the first 10 s and 2 every 10 s after that. Expiring a bucket is only safe once it would be full anyway: set the TTL to at least capacity / refill (25 s here, plus a margin), or evict only buckets whose refilled tokens reach the capacity. The misconception is that cleanup is invisible: forgetting state that is not at its default value changes the decisions the state was there to make.

challenges.name: per-learner-submission-rate-limit
challenges.title: Token buckets per learner, per anonymous IP, with an exam-day override
challenges.description: On the mock exam day a per-IP limit on POST /submissions gave a university lab 1,870 responses 429 while one learner's userscript re-submitted every 200 ms without a single one. Implement class SubmissionRateLimiter(config) for the CodeDev API, on a fake clock in milliseconds (`now` never goes backwards). check(req, now) returns { status, retryAfterSec, remaining }. (1) Sweep first: remove every stored bucket idle for at least config.idleTtlMs (now minus its last request) that would also be full at `now` (its refilled tokens reach the capacity in force); a bucket that is not full must stay, so eviction never changes a decision. (2) Key: a non-empty string userId -> bucket "user:<userId>" with config.user; otherwise a non-empty string ip -> bucket "ip:<ip>" with config.anonymous; otherwise { status: 400, retryAfterSec: null, remaining: 0 } and no bucket is created. (3) Limits in force: the bucket's own { capacity, refillPerSec }, except while config.examDay is not null and examDay.fromMs <= now < examDay.toMs: then the lower of each (min of the capacities, min of the refill rates). (4) Keep tokens as integer micro-tokens (1 token = 1,000,000); a rate of r tokens per second adds Math.round(r * 1000) micro-tokens per millisecond. A new bucket starts full at the capacity in force; an existing one refills lazily: min(capacity in force, tokens + (now - last request) * rate in force). (5) With at least 1 token: take it and return status 200, retryAfterSec null. Otherwise return status 429 and take nothing; retryAfterSec = milliseconds until 1 whole token at the rate in force, rounded up to whole seconds. remaining = whole tokens left after the decision (floor). Every request, allowed or rejected, updates the bucket's last request time. size() returns the number of stored buckets. Input: { config: { user, anonymous, examDay, idleTtlMs }, requests: [{ at, userId?, ip? }] }. The runner replays the requests in time order and prints { allowed, rejected, invalid, buckets, maxBuckets, results } with one line per request, e.g. "t=500 learner-1@10.20.0.5 429 retry-after=5 remaining=0".
hints: A token bucket only needs two numbers per key: how many tokens it had and when it last saw a request. What must you compute from those two numbers before you can answer any request, including the sweep's question "is this idle bucket full yet?"

Look at three places: the function that picks the limits in force at `now` (the exam-day window is half-open, fromMs <= now < toMs, and it takes the lower of each value), the lazy refill (multiply elapsed milliseconds by an integer rate in micro-tokens, then cap at the capacity in force), and the 429 branch, where the missing micro-tokens divided by the rate give milliseconds and Math.ceil turns them into whole seconds.

A worked trace with a different limit: capacity 3, refill 0.4 per second (400 micro-tokens per ms). Requests at 0, 1, 2 take the 3 tokens (remaining 2, 1, 0). At 3 the bucket holds 400 micro-tokens: 999,600 are missing, 999,600 / 400 = 2,499 ms, so Retry-After is 3 seconds and remaining is 0. At 2,503 the bucket holds 400 + 2,500 x 400 = 1,000,400 and the request is allowed with remaining 0. With idleTtlMs 4,000, that bucket is not evicted at 6,600 (4,097 ms idle but only about 1.6 tokens); it is evicted by a sweep at or after 10,003, when 7,500 ms of refill have filled it back to 3.

tests.name: A learner who clicks Run 7 times in 600 ms: 5 allowed, then 429 until a token refills
Anonymous traffic has a stricter bucket per IP; learners behind the same IP are not limited together
Retry-After rounds partial seconds up, with millisecond refill precision
Exam-day override: the lower of both limits while it lasts, normal limits after it ends
Idle buckets are evicted only once full, so eviction never changes a decision
Invalid requests get 400 and create no bucket; a non-string userId falls back to the IP
Large: exam-day burst, 1,500 requests from 400 learners and 40 anonymous IPs
